You write your domain in Rust and mark it with a handful of attributes. Undra generates idiomatic Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript from the schema those attributes produce, so the UI stays SwiftUI on iOS, Jetpack Compose on Android, React on the web, and React Native. Each platform keeps a local mirror of your state, so reads never cross the language boundary. A write crosses once per transaction, and the core answers with one compact binary change-set that patches every mirror. Where these pages come from. Everything here is digested from the repository: the README, the specification in docs/SPEC.md, the onboarding guide, the benchmark results and the playground app. When a page and the spec disagree, the spec wins; the repository is the record.

State in Undra lives in the Rust core as signals inside stores. Platforms hold a local mirror, reads never cross the boundary, and a write crosses once per transaction.

Everything a platform can see is one of eight kinds of thing, each declared with an attribute. They cross the boundary in one of two ways: by value (copied) or by handle (a reference to something that stays in the core). Concept Declared with Crosses Record #[undra::api] on a struct by value Enum #[undra::api] on an enum, unit or data variants by value Error #[undra::error] on an enum; adds Display and std::error::Error by value Object #[undra::api] on an impl block; methods are sync or async by handle Store an object whose struct has #[undra::store]; its signals are mirrored by handle Port #[undra::port] on a trait; implemented by the platform or by a Rust fake the core calls out to it Query, mutation #[undra::query], #[undra::mutation] on an async fn managed by the query client Function #[undra::api] on a free fn like a method with no receiver The rest of this page is about stores, because that is where reactive state lives.

A store is a struct of signals with an impl block that says what the platforms can call. The to-do list from the playground is a complete example: core/src/todos.rs #[undra::store(restore = "Self::assemble")] pub struct Todos { next: AtomicU64, // private state: not a signal #[undra(key = "id")] todos: Signal<Vec<Todo>>, // signal 0 filter: Signal<Filter>, // signal 1 #[undra(key = "id")] visible: DerivedList<Todo>, // signal 2, a view of todos remaining: Computed<u32>, // signal 3, derived } #[undra::api(store)] impl Todos { pub fn new(ctx: Ctx) -> Self { /* … */ } pub async fn add(&self, title: String) -> Result<Todo, TodoError> { /* … */ } pub fn toggle(&self, id: Uuid) { /* … */ } pub fn set_filter(&self, filter: Filter) { self.filter.set(filter); } } A few rules worth knowing up front: Signals are the fields of type Signal<T>, Computed<T> and DerivedList<T>, numbered in declaration order (0, 1, 2, …). Other fields are private state: a Ctx, a counter, configuration. A store needs a constructor, a pub fn returning Self or Result<Self, E>. Generated code calls it to create the object in the core and gets back a handle. Receivers are &self. Objects are shared, so mutation goes …

A Signal<T> holds a value. You read it with get() (a clone) or with(|v| …) (a borrow), and write it with set(value) or update(|v| …). rust self.filter.set(Filter::Done); // replace self.todos.update(|list| list.retain(|t| !t.done)); // edit in place let open = self.todos.with(|list| list.iter().filter(|t| !t.done).count()); A write outside a transaction is an implicit single-write transaction, so the change is committed and delivered at once. Inside update, the closure holds the value's write lock: it must not read or write the same signal, or read a computed derived from it. A violation panics with a clear message instead of deadlocking.

A Computed<T> is a value derived from signals. You name its inputs and give it a function of them: rust let parity = Computed::new(&count, |n| if n % 2 == 0 { Parity::Even } else { Parity::Odd }); let summary = Computed::new((&count, &changes), |(n, changes)| format!("{n} after {changes} changes")); Inputs are &Signal<A> or &Computed<A>, or a tuple of up to six of them, and the closure receives references. A computed is recomputed in the core, in dependency order, and pushed in the same change-set as the write that caused it. The UI never derives anything itself, so it cannot disagree with the core about, say, how many items are left. A computed list is recomputed and sent whole on every change of its inputs. For a filtered or sorted view of a keyed list, use a derived list, which costs the change instead. Because a store with computeds cannot be rebuilt from its plain signals automatically, you name a function that assembles it: #[undra::store(restore = "Self::assemble")]. The macro tells you when you forget (E0013).

When several signals change together, group the writes. Everything inside ctx.txn commits as one transaction, so observers see one consistent change-set and never a half-applied state. The playground's counter changes two signals and derives a third: core/src/counter.rs pub fn add(&self, amount: i32) { self.ctx.txn(|| { self.count.update(|c| *c = c.saturating_add(amount)); self.changes.update(|n| *n = n.saturating_add(1)); }); // one change-set carries count, changes and parity } Transactions nest: an inner txn joins the outer one. A change-set is never split, and change-sets are delivered in commit order; for one store they reach the platform one at a time with strictly increasing transaction ids.

A platform does not receive everything. It observes signals, and only observed signals that changed are sent. Two details follow from that: Observing sends the current value right away, before the call returns in-process, so a store's initial state arrives as an ordinary change-set. A signal written while unobserved is remembered as pending and sent when someone starts observing it. Only what changed is sent. Writing filter in the to-do store ships filter and the rows that entered or left visible, and nothing else, because todos did not change. A signal marked #[undra(no_coalesce)] is delivered on every commit instead of being folded into the latest value. A change-set is a compact binary structure, described on the architecture page. For side effects that belong in the core, Effect::new(deps, f) runs f after each commit that dirtied one of its dependencies, and is cancelled when dropped.

A Signal<Vec<T>> marked #[undra(key = "field")] is a keyed list. The key is the identity of a row, and the core sends changes to it as a patch of positional operations instead of the whole list. Operation Meaning Insert { index, item } put the item at index Remove { index } take the row at index out Update { index, item } replace the row at index Move { from, to } take the row at from, then place it so it ends at to Clear empty the list The platform applies the operations in order to its own copy of the list. If a patch ever disagrees with that copy (an index out of bounds), the platform treats the signal as out of sync and observes it again, which resends the full value.

h: Why a list write costs the change, not the list
x: How the core produces the patch decides the cost. There are two ways. Recorded operations are the fast path. Signal<Vec<T>> has push, insert, remove, update_at, move_item and clear. Each one mutates the list and appends the operation it performed to a log; at commit, that log is the patch. No key is hashed and no item is compared, so the cost is the change, not the length of the list. examples/playground/core/src/biglist.rs /// Inserts a new row so that it ends at `index`. One keyed `Insert`. pub fn insert_at(&self, index: u32, label: String) -> Result<u32, ListError> { // …check the index… let id = self.next_id.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); self.items.insert(index as usize, Item { id, label, version: 0 }); Ok(id) } Raw writes (set, update, replace) are the fallback. They are always correct, but the core cannot know what you did, so at commit it diffs the new list against what the platform has: hash every key, compare the surviving rows. That is O(list). It also falls back to sending the whole value when the two lists share no key, a key occurs twice, or more than half of the old rows were removed. The difference is measured. A DerivedList<T> is a filtered, sorted or mapped view of a keyed list, and it costs the change, not the list. You build it from the list with a pipeline: core/src/todos.rs let visible = todos.derive().filter_with(&filter, |filter, todo| filter.matches(todo)).build(); let remaining = todos.derive().filter(|todo| !todo.done).count(); // a Computed<u32> Its value is always the obvious one: the rows that pass, mapped, then sorted stably by key (filter, filter_with, map, at most one sort_by_key; equal keys keep the list's order). But it is never recomputed. It replays the list's recorded operations on an index of its own, O(log n) each, and the platform receives each as at most two patch operations: a row that enters or leaves the filter is an Insert or a Remove, a row whose sort key changes a Move and an Update (so lists animate it), a change the filter hides nothing at all. The platforms see a read-only keyed list, generated exactly like a computed list. Each platform runtime holds a mirror: store handle, then signal id, then the decoded value. Generated code exposes the mirror in the platform's own idiom (an @Observable property, a StateFlow, a Signal with useSignal), so reading is a local memory read that never calls into the core. Every change-set is applied on the main thread, in one hop per transaction: Swift on the MainActor, Kotlin on Dispatchers.Main.immediate, and TypeScript in a queued flush on the page's main thread. A store is an object with a lifetime: release it explicitly with close() (Swift and Kotlin use deinit and a Cleaner as backstops, TypeScript a FinalizationRegistry), and UndraCore.stats() shows live handle counts.

The core can snapshot every store's plain signals (computeds are left out and recomputed) and restore them, which is how a web page recovers after a crash and how tests rebuild state. Restore keeps the same handles valid, so the platform's references keep working, and it cancels calls that were running on the stores it replaced. This is why the restore function above rebuilds computeds from signals, and why the to-do store continues its id counter above the largest id in the snapshot.

The core reads no clock and no random source and starts no thread of its own. Time comes from the Clock port, delays from ctx.sleep (which goes through the Timer port), randomness from Rng, the network from Http. That is rule R12, and it is why every scenario can be driven with deterministic fakes in Rust and with in-memory adapters on each platform. The to-do store's ids come from a counter for the same reason. See Ports & adapters.
Data fetching, caching and offline behaviour are not something each platform reimplements. They live in the core, next to the state they feed, and every platform observes the same cache.

h: Why the data layer is in the core
x: Fetching, caching, retrying, optimistic updates and offline queues are logic, and logic is what Undra writes once. The core never opens a socket: every request goes through the Http port, which is URLSession, HttpURLConnection or fetch in an app and a scripted fake in a test. The query client keeps one cache that all platforms observe, so the to-do list on the iPhone and the one in a Chrome tab agree about what is fresh.

A query is an async fn whose first parameter is the Ctx, marked with #[undra::query]. This is the playground's remote to-do list, a GET that is cached per list: core/src/remote.rs /// The items of the server's list `list`: `GET {base}/lists/{list}/todos`. #[undra::query(key = "remote-todos:{list}", stale = "30s", persist, retry = 1)] pub async fn remote_todos(ctx: &Ctx, list: String) -> Result<Vec<RemoteTodo>, RemoteError> { let url = endpoint(ctx, &format!("/lists/{list}/todos"))?; parse(&send(ctx, HttpRequest::get(url)).await?) } Argument Meaning key = "…" the cache key; {param} placeholders name parameters, so two lists are two independent entries stale = "30s" how long a successful result stays fresh persist write the entry to the Kv port so it survives a restart retry = 3 how many times to retry a failed fetch idempotent (mutations) the request is safe to repeat, which makes it eligible for the offline queue The signature is checked when you compile: it must be async, take ctx: &Ctx first, and return Result<T, E>. A query whose success value is () or an Option is rejected, because a query caches a value and effects belong in a mutation (E0040 to E0042).

Platforms observe a query through a generated query handle, which is an ordinary store. For remote_todos it is RemoteTodosQueryHandle, and it has five signals: Signal Holds data the latest successful result, or nothing yet status idle, fetching, success or error error the error of the latest failed fetch, cleared by the next success fetching whether a request is in flight, also true while refetching stale data updatedAt when data last changed Constructing the handle registers an observer and starts a fetch if the entry is missing or stale. Releasing it removes the observer; when the last observer goes, the in-flight fetch is cancelled and the entry is kept for five minutes before it is garbage collected. The handle also has refetch() (fetch now, even if fresh) and invalidate() (mark stale; it refetches while observed). tsx const inbox = await RemoteTodosQueryHandle.create("inbox"); // observe const items = useSignal(inbox.data); // in a component const busy = useSignal(inbox.fetching);

An observed entry refetches when it is stale and something happens: an observer is added while it is stale, the app becomes Active again (the Lifecycle port), connectivity returns (the Connectivity port), its optional interval elapses, or it is invalidated, by key prefix. One fetch per key at a time. If five screens observe the same list, they share one in-flight request. Polling and paging. interval = "30s" refetches an observed query on a schedule (Polling), and infinite turns a cursor query into a keyed list that grows by the page (Paging and lazy lists).

A failed fetch is retried retry times (three by default) with exponential backoff, min(1000 × 2ⁿ, 30000) milliseconds, with plus or minus 20% jitter. The jitter comes from the Rng port and the delay from the Timer port, so a test with fakes sees exactly the schedule it scripts.

A mutation is an async fn marked #[undra::mutation]. It shares its cache key with the query it affects. Call it through the context: rust ctx.mutate::<PostRemoteTodoMutation>((list, title)) .optimistic(move |cache| { cache.update::<RemoteTodosQuery>((cached,), |items| items.push(placeholder)); }) .invalidates(/* keys to mark stale */) .await optimistic runs inside a transaction with typed access to cache entries (get, set, update), so the UI shows the new item at once. On success the invalidates keys are marked stale and refetched if observed, which replaces the placeholder with the server's item. The playground wraps this in create_remote_todo and set_remote_done, which are what its three UIs call.

If the mutation fails, the optimistic write is undone, but only the writes that mutation made. Every cache entry carries a write stamp that changes with each write: an optimistic write, a set, or a fetch result. When a mutation fails, each entry it wrote is restored to what it was before, unless something else has written that entry since. An entry that was written since keeps that write. That rule is what makes concurrent mutations safe: a later optimistic mutation's placeholder survives an earlier mutation's rollback, even on the same entry; a fetch result that arrived in the meantime is newer than the failed closure and is kept; a later mutation that wrote directly on top of the failed one inherits its restore point, so if it fails too the entry goes back to before both. Stamps are compared, never contents, so two writes of equal data are still distinguishable. This behaviour is covered by the optimistic-rollback contract scenario on all three platforms.

A mutation marked idempotent that fails with a network error while the Connectivity port says the device is offline is not lost. It is appended to a persisted queue (the Kv key undra.query.queue2) with its parameters, the fingerprint of their types and an idempotency key, and replayed in order when connectivity returns. The request carries an Idempotency-Key header that stays the same across retries and replays, so a server can tell a repeat from a second item. rust #[undra::mutation(key = "remote-todos:{list}", idempotent)] pub async fn post_remote_todo(ctx: &Ctx, list: String, title: String) -> Result<RemoteTodo, RemoteError> { // … if let Some(key) = undra::query::idempotency_key() { request = request.with_header("Idempotency-Key", key.to_string()); } // … } A mutation that is not idempotent fails immediately when offline. While a queued call waits, the optimistic placeholder stays visible, and the caller's await keeps waiting until the network returns and the request is replayed. A queued call survives an app update: its input is migrated by parameter name, or by a #[undra::migrate] hook. One that cannot be migrated is never dropped; it moves to the dead letters, which …

Entries marked persist are written to the Kv port after each successful fetch (debounced, 250 ms) and read back when the core starts. Each entry carries the fingerprint of its type, so an unrelated change to the core keeps the cache, and an entry whose type changed is migrated by name or, if it cannot be, dropped and refetched. At most 1,000 entries are kept (set_max_persisted_entries), least recently updated first out. Storage can fail: a quota runs out, a device is locked. The Kv port reports it as a StorageError, and the client treats storage as best-effort: a failed write is logged once and retried, a failed read starts the entry empty, and an offline queue that cannot be read is never overwritten or replayed until it can be.

Because the network is a port, a query is tested with a scripted fake and no sockets. FakeHttp answers from rules and records every request, including a flaky endpoint: rust let http = FakeHttp::new(); // two timeouts, then success for ever after http.respond_sequence("https://x.test/a", [Err(HttpError::Timeout), Err(HttpError::Timeout)]); http.respond("https://x.test/a", HttpResponse::new(200, b"ok".to_vec())); Pair it with FakeClock to advance time and ScriptedConnectivity to go offline. The core never touches the outside world directly. Time, randomness, the network, storage and the app's lifecycle all come through ports: traits the platform implements and the core calls.

A port is a Rust trait marked #[undra::port]. The platform implements it (an adapter), or a Rust fake does in a test. The core calls it through the context, for example ctx.http().request(req).await, and does not know or care what is behind it. That is what keeps the core deterministic (rule R12): it has no wall clock, no random source and no threads outside the Clock, Rng and Timer ports and the runtime. There are three kinds, and the kind decides how a call travels: Kind Meaning sync the platform answers before the call returns. A port is sync only if every method is sync async the platform answers later; the core's task waits, and can be cancelled event fire and forget from the platform into the core, such as "connectivity changed"

An unavailable port is a normal outcome, not a bug. A port nobody registered behaves as unavailable, a call can be cancelled, and a host can reply with bytes that do not decode. The core handles all three without panicking: If the port method returns Result<T, E>, the failure becomes an E. HttpError and FsError implement From<PortError>, so an unavailable Http port is Network("the Http port has no adapter registered (E0062: register one, see ..)"), with the code and the link to the fix. Your own error type needs the same conversion, and the macro checks it at compile time (E0033). If the method has no error channel, there is no typed way to say "unavailable", so the call panics with a message that names the port and method and says how to bind one (E0062, in the shape of every diagnostic: what, why, fix, docs link). The runtime contains that panic at the boundary. Give optional ports a Result, or register them.

Mark a trait with #[undra::port]. The macro registers it in the schema and generates a proxy type, so the core calls your trait like any other, and the platform gets a protocol or interface to implement. Ask for the same object twice and you get the same wrapper while the first is alive. A store returned twice is observed once, a list of shelves is a list you can compare, and in Swift the wrapper is Hashable by identity, so ForEach(shelves, id: \.self) works. The reference you hold is given back when the wrapper is closed or collected, once. Hold the wrapper for as long as you use it; close() it to let go early.

An object travels as a parameter or a return, and nowhere else. Not allowed Why An object inside a record, a variant or a store's signal, in a stream item, a query or a mutation a value is copied, compared, saved and merged; an object is none of those. Put the object behind a method (E0064 says so) An object of another core two cores can issue the same handle numbers, so the generated code refuses it before anything is sent: UndraCallError.refused An object in a port's parameter or return pass a record or an id instead

An object a method returned is not part of a saved snapshot: after a restore (a web worker crash, undra dev reloading the core) its handle is stale, and calling the method again returns it. Constructed stores restore as before, and so do query handles: the snapshot keeps what a handle is made of and the core builds it again when the app first uses it (ADR-059). What a store keeps in a private field is whatever its restore hook rebuilds.

Passing an object lends it. The call holds it until it finishes, so closing the wrapper while a call is in flight is safe. A failed call hands nothing out. An error, a cancel or a panic gives the references it had issued back. A shelf stays alive while you hold it, even if the core drops its own reference. A trait the app implements, so the core can call it: a progress report, a note, a question for the user.

A callback is a trait the app implements. Mark it #[undra::callback], take it as Arc<dyn Trait> in a method or function, and call it from the core like any other trait. By default on the main thread, in the order things happened. A callback joins the same queue as state changes, so a listener sees the stores as they were when the core called it. With background each listener has its own serial executor instead. Either way the core never runs app code inside its own call.

An implementation that throws the method's own error answers the core with it, typed. Any other error is reported through onError and the core sees the app as unavailable. A throw from a fire-and-forget method is only reported. None of it unwinds into the core. When the core stops waiting (the call that was awaiting was cancelled), the task running the implementation is cancelled too: a Swift Task, a Kotlin Job, a TypeScript AbortSignal passed as the last argument.

The core holds the callback until it lets go, so a listener you create inline lives as long as the core uses it. A core that keeps the listener and an app that keeps the core make a cycle across languages. Two ways out: A subscription object. Return something the app closes (watch above): closing it drops the core's hold. A weak wrapper. Hand the core a wrapper that forwards while the target lives and does nothing after. A stream method takes a callback like any other method: the core holds it while the stream runs and lets it go when the stream ends or is dropped. The core never calls a weak wrapper whose target is gone (the question is answered unavailable); if your own code does in Swift, the method throws the error type's Unavailable, and an error type without one stops the app with a message. Generic code crosses as named instantiations: you list the types, the platforms get an ordinary function, record, class or store for each. Data types first; generic functions, objects and stores follow, with the limits.

The schema describes concrete types, so a generic struct or enum is a template that registers nothing, and each use is a named instantiation. The name is yours and stays stable, which is what the generated Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript need. Decimal is an exact decimal number: a 128-bit mantissa and a scale of at most 38, so 19.99 is 1999 with scale 2. It never goes through a float. Each dependency is built without a clock or a randomness feature, so a core that uses them still builds for wasm32, iOS and Android, and still reads no clock of its own. Write the code once over a type parameter, and say which types the platforms get. A generic function becomes a set of overloads; a generic object or store becomes one ordinary class for each alias you declare. Undra's callers are Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript, which cannot call a Rust generic: there is no T at run time to dispatch on. So the core lists the types it is generic over where it declares the code, the macro expands the ordinary function, method, object or store once for each, and the platforms see what you would have written by hand. An error inside one instantiation says which one: "in newest<Todo>". A call with a type that is not listed is the platform compiler's error, naming the overloads that exist: Swift's "no exact matches in call to global function", Kotlin's "none of the following candidates is applicable", TypeScript's "no overload matches this call". The table is on the types page, with what would lift each limit. In short: no open-ended T (every instantiation is listed), one type parameter per function, no generic queries, ports, callbacks or error enums, and no native generics, because the schema and the platforms' dispatch have no type parameters. A generic Page<T> that a function returns is still the named record of the data types.
A feed from a server grows by the page. A big collection in the core is read a window at a time. Neither ships a whole list across the boundary.

"Paging" hides two different problems, and they get different tools. A feed from a server A big collection in the core Where the rows are on a server; the core fetches a page at a time already in the core (a database, a derived view over 50,000 rows) What the screen shows every row loaded so far a window of it Use an infinite query: a keyed list that grows by the page Lazy<T>: the platform pages the core's list on demand

An infinite query is a query with a cursor. The function takes the cursor and returns one page; the handle on each platform shows all the pages loaded so far as one list, keyed by the field you name. Show the Rust code rust #[undra::query(key = "feed/{filter}", infinite, item_key = "id", stale = "1m")] async fn feed( ctx: &Ctx, filter: Filter, #[undra(cursor)] cursor: Option<String>, ) -> Result<undra::query::Page<Post, String>, ApiError> { // `None` is the first page; `Page { items, next }` says where the next one starts. let body = fetch(ctx, filter, cursor).await?; Ok(Page { items: body.posts, next: body.next }) } The cursor is not part of the cache key and not a parameter on the platform. The handle has the five signals of every query and two more, hasNextPage and fetchingNextPage, and data is the list itself, empty before the first page rather than optional. A store field of type Lazy<T> is a list the core owns and the platform reads a window of. The platform is told how many rows there are and which version of the list that is; it asks the core for the pages it needs. Show the code for Rust, Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript rust #[undra::store] pub struct Library { #[undra(key = "id")] books: Lazy<Book>, // 100,000 rows; the platform never receives them whole } #[undra::api(store)] impl Library { pub fn add(&self, title: String) { self.books.push(Book { .. }); } // the recorded API of Signal<Vec<T>> } swift let library = try Library() ScrollView { LazyVStack { // a lazy container: a List would build every row up front ForEach(0..<library.books.count, id: \.self) { i in if let book = library.books[i] { BookRow(book) } else { BookRow.placeholder } // reading requests the page } } } kotlin val library = Library.create() LazyColumn { items(library.books) { index, book -> if (book != null) BookRow(book) else Placeholder() } } // undra-compose ts const library = await Library.create(); const { length, getItem } = useLazyList(library.books); // for TanStack Virtual or react-window: useVirtualizer({ count: length, ... }) and getItem(index) Use a …
An interval on a query refetches it while it is observed. It runs from the end of the last fetch, pauses when the app is away and resumes when it returns.

Add interval to a query and the core refetches it while somebody is looking. Show the code for Rust, Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript rust #[undra::query(key = "prices", interval = "30s")] async fn prices(ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<Vec<Price>, ApiError> { .. } swift let prices = try PricesQueryHandle() // fetches now, then 30 seconds after each fetch ends // a screen that wants fresher data while it is visible: .onAppear { prices.setPollInterval(.seconds(5)) } .onDisappear { prices.setPollInterval(nil) } // back to the query's own 30 seconds kotlin val prices = PricesQueryHandle.create() DisposableEffect(Unit) { prices.setPollInterval(5.seconds); onDispose { prices.setPollInterval(null) } } ts const prices = await PricesQueryHandle.create(); useEffect(() => { void prices.setPollInterval(5000); return () => void prices.setPollInterval(null); }, []); The shortest interval is one second; below that the compiler says to use a stream, which is the tool for real-time data (the opt-in ports have WebSocket and Server-Sent Events).

The next fetch is scheduled one interval after the end of the previous one, whether it succeeded or failed once its retries ran out. A fetch slower than the interval never overlaps the next, and a struggling server is asked less often rather than hammered. Situation What happens Nobody observes the entry no timer; the last observer going away cancels it The app is in the background or inactive paused, unless the query says poll_in_background The device is offline paused The app comes to the front, the network returns the usual triggers fire (a stale entry refetches, going online refetches everything observed) and polling continues from the end of that fetch Several observers the entry polls at the shortest interval any of them asked for, each new observer starting from the attribute's A fetch fails retried with backoff as any query is, then the interval runs from the end; the error shows and the next success clears it Time comes from the Clock and delays from the Timer port, so a test under undra::ports::fakes advances the clock and sees each poll, background pause included. The contract scenario S33 checks it on every platform with real timers.
Live data comes into the core like everything else: through a port. The core reads at its own pace and decides when to reconnect; the platform owns the socket.

WebSocket and Sse are opt-in ports: a core asks for them with a cargo feature, and a core that does not keeps the schema hash and the wasm size it had. Each platform answers with its own client: URLSessionWebSocketTask, the Kotlin runtime's client on the JVM and Android, the browser's WebSocket. core/Cargo.toml [dependencies] undra = { version = "0.1", features = ["websocket", "sse"] }

The core connects, sends and reads. Messages arrive as a stream the core pulls: it asks for 16 at a time, so a core that stops reading stops the socket, on the platforms that can pause one. core/src/chat.rs use undra::ports::ws::{WsConnection, WsError, WsMessage, WsOptions}; let conn = WsConnection::connect(&ctx, "wss://chat.example.com/room", WsOptions::default()).await?; conn.send_text("hello").await?; let mut messages = conn.messages(); while let Some(next) = undra::ports::next(&mut messages).await { match next { Ok(WsMessage::Text(text)) => room.push(text), Ok(WsMessage::Binary(_)) => {} Err(WsError::Closed { code: 1000, .. }) => break, // the server said goodbye Err(error) => return Err(error), } }

What happened The stream ends with the core called close nothing: it simply ends the server sent a close frame Closed { code, reason } the connection dropped Network the server broke the protocol Protocol the upgrade was refused Refused { status } (from connect) Browsers cannot send headers with a WebSocket, so the browser adapter refuses a connect that has some instead of dropping them: put the credential in the URL or a subprotocol.

The port never reconnects on its own: which close codes to retry, how long to wait and what to resend are your app's rules, and they run in the core, where a test drives them with a fake clock. Backoff gives the delay, a weak context sleeps. rust let backoff = Backoff::default(); // 500 ms doubling to 30 s, with jitter from the Rng port let mut attempt = 0; while weak.sleep(backoff.delay(attempt, &*ctx.rng())).await.is_ok() { attempt += 1; // connect again, re-subscribe, reset `attempt` once a message arrives }

sse::subscribe is a stream of events parsed as the HTML standard says. It ends with Ended when the server finishes the response; subscribe again with the last event id to resume. rust let mut events = sse::subscribe(&ctx, "https://api.example.com/feed", vec![], last_id.clone()); while let Some(Ok(event)) = undra::ports::next(&mut events).await { last_id = event.id.clone().or(last_id); feed.apply(event.data); }

FakeWebSocket and FakeSse are scripted servers: accept or refuse, push, close, drop, echo. They record what the core sent and how much it pulled, so backpressure is an assertion. rust let fakes = fakes::install(&t); fakes.web_socket.echo(true); // ... the core connects and sends ... assert!(fakes.web_socket.delivered(conn) <= consumed + 24); On the web the adapters are an opt-in import, @undra/runtime/realtime, so an app that does not use them ships none of them. Design: ADR-047.
Structured local data with SQLite, written once in the core. The platform owns the file and the thread; the core sends bound statements and gets typed rows back.

Db is an opt-in port over the SQLite each platform already has: the system library on iOS, android.database.sqlite on Android, a JDBC driver on the JVM, node:sqlite in Node and wa-sqlite in a worker on the web. The core stays small and never blocks: the platform owns the database and its thread. On the web the files live in the origin private file system, which one tab holds at a time: a second tab of the same app gets Unavailable. core/Cargo.toml [dependencies] undra = { version = "0.1", features = ["db"] }

Migrations are numbered SQL. The platform runs every one the database has not seen yet, in one transaction: if one fails, none of them happened. core/src/notes.rs const MIGRATIONS: &[Migration] = &[ Migration::new(1, "CREATE TABLE notes (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, done INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)"), Migration::new(2, "CREATE INDEX notes_done ON notes (done)"), ]; let db = Database::open(&ctx, "notes", MIGRATIONS).await?;

SQL is a &'static str, so a value can only reach a statement as a bound parameter. Cells come back typed. rust db.execute("INSERT INTO notes (title) VALUES (?)", params![title]).await?; let rows = db.query("SELECT id, title, done FROM notes WHERE done = ?", params![false]).await?; for row in rows.iter() { let id: i64 = row.get("id")?; let title: String = row.get("title")?; }

A transaction commits when its body returns Ok and rolls back on Err, or when its task is dropped half-way. rust db.transaction(|tx| async move { for title in titles { tx.execute("INSERT INTO notes (title) VALUES (?)", params![title]).await?; } Ok(()) }).await?;

Error When Constraint { kind, .. } a UNIQUE, NOT NULL, foreign-key or CHECK constraint failed Busy the database stayed locked past five seconds Migration { version, .. } a migration failed and everything rolled back, or the file is newer than the app Sql a syntax error, a missing table, a cell read as the wrong type Corrupt, Full, Unavailable the file, the disk, or no database to talk to

FakeDb answers by SQL fragment, injects failures and records every statement, migration and transaction, so the core's database logic is tested without a device. rust fakes.db.fail_on("INSERT", DbError::Full); assert_eq!(notes.add("milk".into()).await, Err(DbError::Full)); Design: ADR-048.
The kit runs your real core on fakes and a manual clock, plays a recorded session as a screen state, and replays what a session asked of the platform.

You want Use a screen that reacts, or a cache that goes stale PreviewCore: the real core, its ports faked, time in your hands a state that is slow to reach RecordedCore: a recorded session under the generated stores, no core a test that fails when the core makes another request Replayer: a recording as the script for the ports The same three exist in Swift (UndraTestKit, a product of the UndraRuntime package), Kotlin (com.github.shreypdev.undra:testkit, at the runtime's version), TypeScript (@undra/testkit, the release's undra-testkit-<version>.tgz, no runtime dependencies) and, for tests of the core itself, Rust (undra::testing). They sit beside the runtimes: no generated file, wire frame or C entry point changes.

PreviewCore.load starts your app’s own core in the process with a deterministic fake behind every standard port. A seed fills them; advance moves the clock one deadline at a time and lets the core settle between. Todos(ctx: preview.core) return TodosScreen(todos: todos) .task { for title in ["Buy milk", "Walk the dog"] { _ = try? await todos.add(title: title) } } } Kotlin test val preview = PreviewCore.load(UndraPlaygroundCore::load, Seed.fromJson(seedJson)) val todos = Todos(preview.core) preview.fakes.http.respond("https://api.test/todos", httpResponse(200, "[]")) preview.advance(31_000) // the cached list goes stale; the core refetches Story or Vitest test const preview = await PreviewCore.load({ wasm: "/undra_core.wasm", expectedSchemaHash: UndraIds.schemaHash, seed }); const inbox = await RemoteTodosQueryHandle.create("inbox", preview.core); await preview.advance(31_000); Show a seed one JSON document for every kit seed.json { "version": 1, "now_ms": 1700000000000, "rng_seed": 42, "kv": { …

RecordedCore loads a recording and releases its change-sets with a playhead you move. Calls are answered by the next recorded reply for the same target; a call the recording has no reply for is a typed refusal that names it. Show Swift 3 lines swift let recorded = try RecordedCore.load(Recording(json: text), expectedSchemaHash: UndraIds.schemaHash) let todos = try Todos(ctx: recorded.core) // the recorded constructor reply recorded.advance(ms: 300) // the change-sets up to 300 ms into the session

The dev server sees every call, reply, change-set and port call, on iOS, Android and the web alike, so one flag captures a session. A reload starts a new core, so a new file (session-2.json). bash undra dev --record session.json A recording holds what the app asked the platform and was answered, so it can hold secrets. SecureStore payloads are left out by default (the calls are there, their arguments and replies are empty; --record-secrets keeps them). HTTP headers and bodies, Kv values and files are recorded as they are: do not share a recording of a real account’s session. If the file cannot be written the runner warns once, stops recording and keeps serving. A recording is one canonical JSON document, undra.recording version 1: payloads in hex, handles as strings, times in milliseconds. A recording made on one platform is read by all of them. Show the format an excerpt session.json { "format": "undra.recording", "version": 1, "schema_hash": "0xb5b7b1dc29182a9d", "source": "dev-server", "platform": "ios", "events": [ {"t":100,"kind":"call","target":"constructor","type":4125302698,"method":898850282,"call":1,"args":""}, …

A Replayer answers a core’s port calls from a recording, in order per port. A call that differs is a typed mismatch, an extra one is exhausted, a recorded call with no reply in the file is unanswered, and a recorded call never made is unconsumed. A deviation consumes nothing, so one wrong call does not shift every later answer. Show Swift and Rust 2 snippets Swift let replayer = Replayer(try Recording(json: text)) let core = try UndraPlaygroundCore.load(.inproc(adapters: replayer.adapters())) // ... run the flow ... try replayer.finish() // throws each mismatch, and each recorded call the core never made Rust let replayer = Arc::new(Replayer::new(&Recording::from_json(&text)?)); replayer.install(t.host()); // ... run the core ... replayer.finish().expect("the core made the calls it made when it was recorded");

iOS: three SwiftUI #Previews, built with the app. Android: two Compose @Previews over RecordedCore (the preview pane cannot load a native core); the kit is a debug-only dependency. Web: four stories in Component Story Format, rendered by Vite alone. Storybook loads them unchanged and is not a dependency. The kit uses only public APIs, and CI builds all three. docs/TESTING.md has the full reference: the seed and recording formats, the fakes’ conformance file, and the limits.
An app update changes the core's types while the device still holds data the old version wrote. Undra reads it by name, converts what it can, and refuses the rest out loud.

Three things an app writes can be read by the next version of the app: a snapshot of its stores (crash recovery on the web, undra dev's reload, an app that saves one), the cached results of persist queries, and the offline queue of idempotent mutations. Each records the fingerprint of its types: a hash of exactly the records, enums and fields it holds. A change elsewhere in the core (a new method, a new query, a doc comment) does not move it, so the data is used as it is, with no work at all. When a fingerprint did change, Undra reads the old bytes with the description that was stored next to them and converts them to the new types by name. It never guesses: data that cannot be converted is refused with a typed outcome you can show, never decoded into the wrong values.

These changes need no code. They are the ones most updates are made of: Change What the old data becomes Fields or signals reordered matched by name; order is irrelevant A field added as an Option None A field added with #[undra(default)] its zero value: false, 0, "", empty, the nil UUID, the epoch A store signal added with #[undra(default)] T::default() A field, variant or signal removed dropped Enum variants added or renumbered matched by name An integer widened (i32 to i64, u8 to u32, u16 to i32), f32 to f64 the same value T to Option<T>, Bytes to Vec<u8> or back the same value Any of these inside a Vec, an Option or a map applied to every item Anything else is not structural: a narrowing (i64 to i32), a type change (i32 to String), a renamed field, variant or signal, a variant the new type no longer has, or a new field with no default. Those need a hook.

A hook is a plain function marked #[undra::migrate]. It receives the old value as a DynValue (fields and variants by name) and returns the new one, or a MigrateError to refuse it. There are three kinds: rust use undra::prelude::*; // Any persisted `Todo` whose structure changed, wherever it is. #[undra::migrate(ty = "Todo")] fn todo_from_name(old: &DynValue) -> Result<Todo, MigrateError> { let title = old.field("name").and_then(DynValue::as_str) .ok_or_else(|| MigrateError::new("a todo without a name"))?; Ok(Todo { title: title.to_owned(), done: false }) } // One signal of one store in a snapshot (`None`: the snapshot has no such signal). #[undra::migrate(store = "Profile", signal = "age")] fn age(old: Option<&DynValue>) -> Result<f32, MigrateError> { match old.and_then(DynValue::as_i64) { Some(age) if age >= 0 => Ok(age as f32), Some(age) => Err(MigrateError::new(format!("{age} is not an age"))), None => Ok(18.0), } } // The queued input of one mutation, by parameter name. #[undra::migrate(mutation = "add_todo")] fn add_todo(old: &DynRecord) -> Result<DynRecord, MigrateError> { let mut new = old.clone(); new.rename("name", "title"); Ok(new) } Structural migration is tried first, …

Each kind of data has its own refusal, and none of them loses data silently: Data Outcome A snapshot the restore fails as a whole with RestoreError::Incompatible { store, signal, reason } (restore code 7 on the platforms: UndraRestoreError / UndraRestoreException), the core is unchanged, and the reason is logged. One exception: a store type the new build removed is left out (its handles go stale) and reported. A cached query result deleted, because it can be fetched again; a WARN names the query and the reason A queued mutation never deleted: it moves to the dead letters, and the rest of the queue replays The dead letters are yours to show, export or settle: rust let query = ctx.query(); for letter in query.dead_letters() { log::warn!("{} could not be sent: {}", letter.mutation, letter.reason); // letter.params: the input by parameter name; letter.raw: the bytes as stored } query.retry_dead_letter(key)?; // after an update that added a hook query.discard_dead_letter(key); // for good ctx.query().persist_stats() counts what was migrated, dropped and dead-lettered, and the runtime's statistics carry the same numbers under query.persist.

Build the old and the new core, write the data with one and read it with the other. The playground does exactly this in its contract scenarios: UNDRA_PLAYGROUND_V2=1 undra build builds a second core whose stores, records and mutations changed the way an update does, and every platform checks that a snapshot and a queue written by the first are read by name by the second, and that an incompatible change is refused or dead-lettered. In Rust, a TestRuntime restores a snapshot you build from an edited Schema (its stores_closure is the description an older build would have written).

x: Do not read the generated files in a review. GitHub collapses them, and undra bindgen --check proves they are exactly what the schema generates. x: A line is breaking when code an app wrote against the old bindings can stop compiling or change what it means against the new ones, and additive when it cannot. A removed or changed signature is breaking; an added function, method, store, object or record is additive. An added record field is breaking even with a default: a TypeScript record is an interface, and an object literal that builds one must name every field (Swift and Kotlin default an appended field of a primitive, string, time, optional or collection type). Items are matched by name. x: Show a GitHub Actions job yaml - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: { fetch-depth: 0 } - run: undra bindgen --check --docs # the bindings are what the schema generates - run: undra schema export --check # schema.json is the core's schema - run: undra schema diff --against origin/main --exit-code # fails on a breaking change The first step proves the committed bindings, the second proves the committed schema, and the third turns a breaking change into a decision somebody makes on purpose. Without the third, the diff is for the reviewer to read. To skip committing bindings at all, generate them at build time and ignore the trees; the committed bindings are what a native reviewer's IDE and a Swift package see without running undra, which is why Undra commits them by default.
On the web the core is a wasm module. It can run off the main thread, and when a panic traps it, it can come back from its last snapshot.

mode: "wasm-worker" runs the core in a Web Worker, so a heavy call never blocks the UI. The core calls some ports synchronously (Clock, Rng, Log and any #[undra::port(sync)]) and cannot wait for the main thread, so those are answered in the worker. Clock, Rng and Log need nothing from you. Ports with asynchronous methods (Http, Kv, SecureStore, Fs and your own async ports) run on the main thread, exactly as in wasm-main.

Put them in a small module the worker imports before the core starts, and pass its URL. The same module overrides Clock, Rng or the core's timers in this mode: ts // main.ts const core = await UndraCore.load({ mode: "wasm-worker", wasm, expectedSchemaHash: UndraIds.schemaHash, worker: { ports: new URL("./worker-ports.js", import.meta.url) }, }); // worker-ports.ts: runs inside the worker export default { [UndraIds.Ports.Locale.portId]: localePortImpl({ hello: () => "Bonjour" }), }; export const adapters = { timer: myTimer }; // optional: clock, rng, timer A synchronous port registered on the main thread in this mode is refused when the core loads (UndraError("options"), naming the port), not at its first call. With a bundler, make the module a worker entry.

A native core contains a panic and keeps going. A wasm core cannot: the panic traps the instance. With recovery: crashRecovery() (imported from @undra/runtime, so an app without it ships none of this code), the runtime keeps a snapshot of your stores (at most once a second while they change, in an idle moment, in the worker in worker mode) and restarts from it: ts import { UndraCore, crashRecovery } from "@undra/runtime"; const core = await UndraCore.load({ mode: "wasm-main", wasm, expectedSchemaHash: UndraIds.schemaHash, recovery: crashRecovery(), // or crashRecovery({ snapshotEveryMs, maxSnapshotBytes, maxRestarts, perMs }) onPanic: (report) => crashReporter.send(report), onCoreRestarted: (e) => configureRemote(core, settings), // re-apply core state that is not in a store }); On a trap What your app sees Calls and streams in flight fail with UndraCallError.Unavailable, reason restarted; they may or may not have run and are never retried for you Stores keep their handles and show the snapshot's values Query handles keep their handle and their wrapper (the core re-issues them from the snapshot, and builds each one again when the recovery observes it), then fetch again; one …
A wasm core needs WebCrypto. Without crypto.getRandomValues, load rejects with UndraTransportError("unsupported") rather than run with predictable idempotency keys.

Four things a shipped app needs that nobody should write for themselves: a crash report that names the Rust frame, the symbol files to read it with, a way to finish the offline queue while the app is not on screen, and a core that is as small as a native release build can make it.

A panic in the core never crashes the app: the call that was running fails with UndraCallError.panicked and the core goes on. Your crash reporter still wants to know. Set onPanic when you load the core and it receives one structured report for every panic the core contained (a call, a detached task, a computed, a background task, an init or migration hook), once, in order, on the main thread. Nothing is linked for you: forward the report to the reporter you already use. Without onPanic the runtime logs one line, so a panic is never silent. Field What it holds The panic message and location (file:line:column; release builds remap your home directory to ~, so no path names your machine). The context operation, what was running (Todos.add, task, computed Todos.visible), and the Rust thread. The backtrace frames, innermost first, at most 48. Always the address of each instruction as an offset into the core's image; a debug build also has symbol, file and line. The build namespace, coreVersion and schemaHash: which core. The image imageId: the Mach-O UUID, ELF build id or wasm SHA-256 of the image the addresses belong to, which is what symbol files are keyed by. Show the three loaders …

The OS gives an app a window to work in while it is not on screen: iOS BGTaskScheduler, Android WorkManager, a page about to hide. The core spends it on what is worth finishing: the offline queue replays, stale queries refetch, and what waits to be written is written. The platform calls runInBackground with the window it was given; the core runs its background tasks inside it and reports back. Report Meaning Finished finished: every task was done in time and nothing is pending. Tell the OS it succeeded only then. Work done replayed queued mutations sent, refetched queries fetched again. Work left stillPending: queued mutations and unfinished fetches. A run returns when its tasks are done, or half a second before the deadline so you can still tell the OS. Whatever a task did stays done: the queue persists per item, a request in flight is the client's and goes on, so a run that is cut short, or cancelled when the OS takes the window back, loses nothing and sends nothing twice. Most apps need one core. When a second one arrives, a vendor's SDK or a module another team ships, the two load into the same app side by side, each under its own namespace.

Put the app's domain in one core and split it into crates inside it. Add a second core only for code that ships on its own. One core, several crates Several cores State and transactions shared: one store graph, one order of writes separate: each core has its own Releases together each on its own schedule Cost one runtime a runtime, its threads and a copy of Undra per core

A core's namespace names everything it exports, so two cores never collide. By default it is the core's package name in snake case; set it in undra.toml (lowercase letters, digits and _, at most 32 characters). undra.toml [core] path = "core" namespace = "acme_pay" What Named The C symbol, which returns the core's table acme_pay_undra_api iOS AcmePayCore.xcframework, one prelinked libacme_pay.a per slice Android libacme_pay.so Web acme_pay.wasm The bindings' entry, in Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript UndraAcmePay undra build refuses a namespace that a sibling project already uses, and every runtime refuses to load two cores with one. The namespace also keeps the default storage apart: each core's Kv, SecureStore, Fs and Db live under undra/<namespace>/ on every platform, so two cores that use the defaults never see each other's data unless you hand them one adapter of your own.

Load each core once, through its own entry. Every generated type defaults to the core of its own package, so a call never reaches the wrong one. Where a token lives, when it is refreshed and what logging out forgets are rules of the app, not of three UIs. Written once in the core, they hold on iOS, Android and the web.

The session is a signal. Auth.session is SignedOut or SignedIn. The root view switches on it; nothing else decides which screen shows. Tokens are secrets, not state. They go to the SecureStore port (Keychain, Android Keystore, WebCrypto) and never into a signal, because every signal is mirrored into each platform's memory. A 401 is not an error. authed adds the token and, on a 401, refreshes once and retries. A second request that meets the same 401 waits for the refresh in flight. A refresh the server refuses signs the user out, wherever the request came from. Queued writes use today's token. An offline write replayed an hour later goes through authed too, so it carries the token that is current then. Logout forgets. Both tokens, the persisted cache, the session. It is refused with a typed PendingWrites while writes wait in the offline queue: they would go out as whoever signs in next. Sign-in puts the tokens in SecureStore and nothing in plain storage. A 401 costs exactly one refresh and the caller never sees it; a refused refresh clears both tokens, the persisted cache and the screen. A request that meets a refresh in progress waits instead of refreshing again. A session left by the last run resumes (refreshing on the way); sign-out is refused while a write is queued.

The query client has no clear() yet. Sign-out deletes the persisted entries and the recipe keys cached data by user (profile:{user}), so the next person never reads the last one's entry; in-memory entries leave with their observers. The core cannot show a login web view or an OAuth sheet: that is the platform's. It hands the code to sign_in like any other value. Source: examples/cookbook/core/src/auth.rs. Pages append until the server says there are no more, and then a scroll view's calls send nothing. A failed page keeps the cursor, so the retry continues from the same place. A page reaches the platforms as one change-set of inserts, for the list and for the view (decoded from the wire, as a platform sees it). The topic filters the view, and pages loaded later join it.

The core reads the file through Fs, sends it in parts through Http and shows progress as a signal. The offline queue does the retrying, so no part of the recipe asks whether the network is up.

A part is a mutation. put_part is idempotent, so while the device is offline it waits in the persisted queue and is replayed when the network returns, with the same Idempotency-Key. The upload just awaits it. Progress is a patch. uploads is a keyed list; every acknowledged part is a one-row update of sent and total, which is a progress bar. One part in the queue at a time. The queue stores a part's bytes, so memory and disk cost one part, not the file. Retry resumes. A part the server refuses fails the upload with the reason in its row. retry reads the file again and continues from the first part the server has not acknowledged. The server's name for the upload comes from the Rng port: random in an app, seeded in a test. A 150,000-byte file goes up as three parts and the screen sees 0, 64 KiB, 128 KiB, then all of it. Offline, the upload waits with one part in the queue; when the network returns it finishes, and the queue is empty. A refused second part fails the upload at 64 KiB; retry sends parts 1 and 2 and never part 0.

The Http port has no streaming body and Fs reads a file whole, so the recipe suits photos and documents, not a multi-hundred-megabyte video. The queue replays while the app runs, and in the windows the OS gives a background run (BGTaskScheduler, WorkManager). Undra does not hand the transfer itself to the OS, so a part is sent only while the app or one of those windows is alive. Progress is per acknowledged part, not per byte on the wire. Source: examples/cookbook/core/src/upload.rs.
The platform owns the socket; the core owns the policy. Which close to retry, how long to wait and what to resend are written once, in Rust, and tested with a fake clock.

One task. Live::start spawns it. It connects, reads, and when the connection ends sleeps Backoff (500 ms doubling to 30 s, jitter from the Rng port) on the Timer port, then connects again. Every end is typed. A refused upgrade with 401 or 403 stops for good, because the credentials are the problem. A normal close (1000) is a goodbye. Anything else is retried. A server that accepts and drops keeps backing off: the attempt count resets when a message arrives, not when the socket opens. Fallback. Every third failed attempt the core tries server-sent events (Fallback), resuming from the last event id, for networks that cut WebSockets. Backpressure is the core's pace. Messages are a stream the core pulls, sixteen at a time: a core that stops reading stops the socket, on the platforms that can pause one. The UI observes link (idle, open, reconnecting, fallback, stopped) and the keyed list messages like any store. It never sees a socket. The platform's job is the adapter: URLSessionWebSocketTask, the Kotlin runtime's client, the browser's WebSocket.

A dropped connection shows Reconnecting and opens again after the backoff; the wait doubles while the server stays down. Refused credentials stop for good (two minutes of fake time, no new connection); a 1000 close is a goodbye. A network that cuts WebSockets reaches the event stream on the third attempt, and the next stream resumes with the last event id. send needs an open connection; stop closes with 1000 and does not come back; the list keeps the last hundred.

WebSocket and Sse are opt-in ports (WebSocket & server-sent events): the module is behind the cookbook's realtime feature. A message sent while the link is down is not queued: presence and chat are facts about now. Anything that must arrive is a mutation. A browser cannot send headers on a WebSocket, so a credential goes in the URL or a subprotocol. Source: examples/cookbook/core/src/realtime.rs.
Offline-first is three decisions the core makes once: reads come from disk, writes queue, and an update never loses what the last build left on the device.

Reads come from disk. notes is a persist query: the list is on screen from the first frame of the next launch, and refreshed in the background. Your app already has one: a token it refreshes, interceptors, tracing, certificate pinning. Hand it to the core's network ports and every request the core makes goes through it, with nothing Undra-specific to configure.

The core never makes a request; the platform does, through the Http port (and WebSocket and Sse where the core asks for them). The default adapters use the platform's own client. That is not your client: on Android HttpURLConnection is OkHttp underneath, but the platform's instance, so a request from the core carries no token, shows in no trace and is not pinned. The fix is not an adapter of your own (the contract is hundreds of lines: typed errors, a timeout that covers the body, cancellation that closes the socket, streams that stop the server when the core stops reading). It is passing your client to the adapter that already is that contract.

Android: add the optional okhttp-adapters module (com.github.shreypdev.undra:okhttp-adapters, at the runtime's version) and call AndroidPlatformDefaults.installWithOkHttp(core, context, client) in place of install. Http, WebSocket and Sse go through your OkHttpClient: its interceptors, its Authenticator (a 401 is answered with a refreshed token and the request goes again), its event listeners, its CertificatePinner. One exception is OkHttp's own: a WebSocket's upgrade is seen by your application interceptors, not by your network interceptors or your event listener. iOS: pass your URLSession to HttpAdapter, URLSessionWebSocketAdapter and URLSessionSseAdapter. Its configuration, its delegate (server trust and the pinning built on it, authentication challenges) and its URLProtocol classes apply. Give event streams a session with the same delegate and a configuration that lets a stream stay quiet. Web: pass your fetch and WebSocket to fetchHttp, fetchSse and browserWebSocket. Whatever your wrapper does to a request, it does to the core's. React Native: nothing to pass. reactNativeHttp() is React Native's fetch, which is the app's networking module, so what the app configures there …

h: What goes through your stack, and what is yours
x: Port Kotlin on OkHttp Swift on URLSession Http the whole call, as the app's own requests go the whole task WebSocket the upgrade request (OkHttp gives its listener no WebSocket events) the upgrade: the connection is a task of your session Sse the request, on a client derived from yours with no read timeout and HTTP/1.1 the request, on the session you give the Sse adapter What your client decides stays yours: redirects, retries, the timeouts when a request has none of its own, compression, caching, how many calls run at once (the core's requests wait their turn with yours). The core's contract holds on top: an error status is a response, a failure is a typed error, the request's own timeout bounds the whole exchange, cancelling the call closes the socket.

Kotlin: the Http, WebSocket and Sse contract suites that run on the default adapters run on OkHttp's too, on the JVM and on a device. An interceptor sees every request and changes a header, an Authenticator refreshes a token and the request, its body included, goes again, an event listener sees each call, and the recipe's client above is run against a local server. Swift: the WebSocket suite runs a second time on an app's session, and Http, Sse and WebSocket are shown to carry the session's configuration and to reach its delegate. TypeScript: a wrapped fetch sees every request, adds a header and answers a 401 with a refreshed token; an app's WebSocket constructor adds a token to the upgrade.

OkHttp's WebSocket repairs malformed UTF-8 in a text frame (U+FFFD) where the default adapter fails the connection with close code 1007; keep ClientWebSocketAdapter for the port if you need the check. The default OkHttp client follows redirects from https to http; the other adapters never do. followSslRedirects(false) gives the same rule. The Kotlin lines are compiled and tested with the okhttp-adapters module (they need OkHttp, which the other modules never carry); the Swift and TypeScript lines are checked like the rest of the cookbook. Granularity. Observation redraws a view when a property it read changes; an ObservableObject redraws every view that observes the store when any of its properties changes. SwiftUI coalesces the events of one drain into one update. Split a big store, or observe a smaller one. A big list is copied on every patch. @Published has no in-place accessor, so a keyed patch to a list copies the array once, where Observation mutates it in place. Measured on an Apple M5 Pro (release build, 32-byte rows): about 5 µs for 1,000 rows, 48 µs for 10,000 and 0.5 ms for 100,000, against 0.2 µs at any size under Observation. It is linear in the list and paid once per applied patch, not per op (the mirror merges a frame's patches into one apply, so 100 ops cost about what 1 does). It is invisible for lists of thousands; for 100,000 rows that change every frame, page the list or observe a smaller store. One name. A store member called objectWillChange is E0051 in this mode, because ObservableObject declares it. SQLite change counts. The built-in SQLiteDbAdapter counts changes with sqlite3_changes, a C int (the 64-bit one needs iOS 15.4): a single statement that changes more than 2,147,483,647 rows …

One schema feeds three generators. Three runtimes hold the mirrors. A small binary wire carries writes in and change-sets out. This page is the tour, and the specification in the repository is the contract.

Undra is a Rust core, a schema extracted from it, three code generators, and three platform runtimes. Your screens sit on generated bindings; the bindings sit on a runtime package; the runtime talks to the core through a transport that is an ABI, not a framework. Each platform has the same four layers; only the bottom one is platform-specific machinery. React Native shares the web's two middle layers. The core is one codebase. On each platform it is linked the way that platform expects: a prelinked static library in an XCFramework on iOS, a .so over JNI on Android, a wasm module on the web, each named after the core's namespace and reached through one table of entry points, so an app can carry more than one core. A React Native app links the iOS and Android builds as they are and reaches them from JavaScript through JSI, under the same generated package and @undra/runtime as the web (React Native). During development the same core can instead run on your machine behind a WebSocket (undra dev).

Everything is derived from the schema. Bindgen emits three trees that depend only on the matching runtime package. Everything starts with the macros. #[undra::api], #[undra::store], #[undra::port] and friends validate your code and register a description of each public type and function. Collected together, those descriptions are the schema: records, enums, objects, stores with their signals, functions, ports and queries. The CLI builds your core as a host library, loads it, asks for the schema, and hands it to undra bindgen, which writes a Swift package, a Gradle module and an npm package. Generated code depends only on the matching runtime package. Three properties of this design are worth stating plainly: Names become ids at compile time. A type id is a hash of its name, a method id a hash of Type.method, a port id a hash of port.Trait, and a signal id is its position among the store's signal fields. Every platform agrees without a registry lookup. The hash is FNV-1a. The schema has a hash. One mutator. The core has one lock. Whoever holds it is the core loop. A synchronous call from the host runs on the caller's thread holding that lock, so it costs a mutex acquire, not a thread hop. Async work. Async calls are tasks on a small executor with no tokio, polled by the core thread, one task per in-flight call. Cancelling a call drops its future. A blocking pool runs blocking work off the lock. It must not write signals, and debug builds refuse such writes. wasm is single threaded. The host calls undra_poll() on the next microtask whenever the core asks to be scheduled. Shutdown is orderly. Every call still in flight is answered as cancelled and every stream ends, each exactly once, before the threads are joined.

Generated Swift is written the way a Swift engineer would write it by hand: value types, error enums you catch by case, async/await, AsyncSequence and an @Observable store. Swift 6 language mode, strict concurrency, no Objective-C. undra bindgen writes a Swift package (Sources/<Module>/Generated/*.swift and a Package.swift) that depends only on UndraRuntime. The shapes below come from the playground's generated code and the specification (§10.1). Reference. Every declaration the playground generates, with its docs, is in the Swift reference.

Load the core once, before any store is created, through the entry generated for it: Undra and the core's namespace ([core] namespace in undra.toml, by default the core's package name), here UndraPlaygroundCore. It checks the core's schema hash against the one the bindings were generated from and throws a clear error if they differ. UndraBootstrap.swift import UndraRuntime import PlaygroundCore @MainActor static func start() throws { let adapters = Adapters.platformDefault // URLSession, Keychain, files, … .replacing(PlaygroundNetwork.shared) // swap one port try UndraPlaygroundCore.load(.inproc(adapters: adapters)) } In debug builds you can attach to the core that undra dev serves instead, with UndraPlaygroundCore.load(.remote(url: url, adapters: adapters)). After loading, every generated type defaults to its entry's core: try Todos() is try Todos(ctx: UndraPlaygroundCore.core). Before the core is loaded, or after shutdown(), that is a shut-down placeholder: constructors throw UndraCallError.unavailable(.closed) instead of stopping the app, and the first use logs what to do. The core links like any static library, with no -force_load, so an app can carry more than one.

The ten standard ports are implemented by UndraRuntime (URLSession, Keychain, FileManager, NWPathMonitor and so on) and are not generated into your module. A port you define yourself becomes a protocol your app implements and registers with the adapters: swift public protocol Http: UndraPort { func request(_ req: HttpRequest) async throws(HttpError) -> HttpResponse } See Ports & adapters for the defaults and for swapping one.

Change-sets are applied on the MainActor, in one hop per transaction, so observable properties only ever change on the main thread. Stores and objects release their handle on close(), with deinit as the backstop. UndraCore.stats() exposes live handle counts for tests. Swift 6 strict concurrency is on. Generated stores are @MainActor; objects are @unchecked Sendable because the core serializes access behind its lock.

Generated Kotlin is what a Kotlin engineer would write by hand: data classes, sealed hierarchies, suspend functions, Flow, and StateFlows you read with collectAsState(). The runtime needs only the standard library and kotlinx-coroutines. undra bindgen writes a Gradle module (src/main/kotlin/<package>/*.kt, a build.gradle.kts and a .gitignore) that depends only on undra-runtime. A store extends UndraStore. Every signal is a read-only StateFlow; computed signals are updated by the core. Read them in Compose with collectAsState(), no extra module needed. kotlin class Todos : UndraStore { val todos: StateFlow<List<Todo>> val filter: StateFlow<Filter> val visible: StateFlow<List<Todo>> // computed by the core val remaining: StateFlow<UInt> // computed by the core constructor(ctx: UndraCore = UndraPlaygroundCore.core) fun setFilter(f: Filter) // a command suspend fun add(title: String): Todo // throws TodoError } kotlin @Composable fun TodosScreen(vm: TodosViewModel = viewModel()) { val visible by vm.store.visible.collectAsState() val remaining by vm.store.remaining.collectAsState() Text("$remaining left") LazyColumn { // the list is keyed by id in the core, so Compose moves and animates rows items(visible, key = { it.id }) { todo -> TodoRow(todo) } } } Hold on to the store. The runtime's mirror holds a store weakly. A StateFlow on its own does not keep the store, and the core object behind it, alive. Keep the store in a ViewModel and close it in onCleared().

The ten standard ports are implemented in dev.undra.runtime.adapters and, for Android, in the android-adapters module (HttpURLConnection, files, an Android Keystore key, ConnectivityManager, activity lifecycle callbacks and so on; AndroidPlatformDefaults.install(core, context) registers them all) and are not generated into your module. Android-specific adapters live in the android-adapters module, not in the runtime.

Signals are updated on Dispatchers.Main.immediate, in one hop per transaction. On a JVM without Android the runtime falls back to a single-thread executor, which is what the JVM test suite uses. UndraStore and UndraObject implement AutoCloseable. Call close() to release the handle (a use { } block works); a Cleaner releases leaked handles as a backstop. UndraCore.stats() exposes live handle counts. Over JNI, callbacks arrive from core threads and are decoded immediately; you never see a raw buffer.

An object is a class holding a handle. Every method returns a Promise, which keeps the API uniform across main-thread, worker and remote modes. A command's promise resolves even when the call fails (see Errors), and a stream method returns an AsyncIterable that fails with the same errors while you iterate it. A store extends UndraStore. Every signal is a read-only Signal<T>: get() returns the current value, peek() reads without subscribing, and subscribe(fn) calls you on change and returns an unsubscribe function. Computed signals are written by the core. ts export class Todos extends UndraStore { readonly todos: Signal<Todo[]>; readonly filter: Signal<Filter>; readonly visible: Signal<Todo[]>; // computed by the core readonly remaining: Signal<number>; // computed by the core static create(core?: UndraCore): Promise<Todos>; setFilter(f: Filter): Promise<void>; // a command: never rejects add(title: string, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<Todo>; } Change-sets are batched with queueMicrotask into one flush per macrotask, so several signals that changed in one transaction update together and a component never renders a half-applied state.

@undra/runtime/react exports two hooks. useSignal is useSyncExternalStore over a signal, with a server snapshot. useUndra creates a store when the component mounts and closes it when it unmounts; it returns undefined until the store exists, and useSignal accepts an undefined signal. tsx import { useUndra, useSignal } from "@undra/runtime/react"; export function CounterView() { const counter = useUndra(Counter); // undefined until created const count = useSignal(counter?.count); const parity = useSignal(counter?.parity); // computed in the core, same change-set if (counter === undefined) return null; return <button onClick={() => void counter.increment()}>{count} ({parity})</button>; } Adapters ship for the other frameworks as thin files, exported from @undra/runtime/vue (useSignal as a shallowRef, useUndra), /svelte (signalStore, a Readable) and /solid (useSignal as an Accessor, useUndra). The frameworks are optional peer dependencies; the core package imports none of them.

h: The SSE adapter read a byte at a time

x: Nothing gated a native core's size. iOS and Android release builds now use a profile at opt-level = "s" that keeps the four crates of the call path at full speed, and three gates hold the hello world: 898,176 bytes for arm64-v8a and 960,776 for x86_64 (stripped, uncompressed) against 1.2 MB, and an iOS slice of 784,086 against 900 KB. We did not have the reported core, so we estimated where it lands: the hello world's share plus the rest, scaled by how much the playground shrinks. p: A week of outside use: seven findings, five fixes
x: The default Android adapter used HttpURLConnection. An app's token refresh, interceptors, tracing and certificate pinning live in its own OkHttpClient, an object the platform's HttpURLConnection cannot reach, so a request from the core carried no token, appeared in no trace and was not pinned. The optional okhttp-adapters module puts Http, WebSocket and SSE over the app's own client with one call; on iOS the app's URLSession serves all three. Two limits remain. OkHttp itself leaves a client's network interceptors and event listener out of a WebSocket upgrade, so tracing written that way will not see the core's WebSockets; the docs say so. And the SSE adapter refuses a background URLSession while the WebSocket adapter does not yet, which is on the roadmap. The review's High: in the old install order, a queued offline request could leave through the default adapter, without the token and without the pin.

p: Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works
x: Every cross-language framework has to decide what crosses the boundary, how often, and what it costs. Undra's answer fits in a sentence: reads never cross the boundary, and writes cross once per transaction. This post walks through the mechanism with real generated code from the playground app, the numbers we measured with links to the raw results, and an honest section on what the design costs you. 30 Sep 2026 · 14 min read · Undra team

p: Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works
x: There are roughly three ways to keep native UI in step with state that lives in another language. The UI can ask for each value when it needs it, which costs a crossing per read per render. The core can send the whole state after every change, which costs a crossing proportional to the state. Or the UI can hold a copy, and the core can send only what changed. Undra does the third, and states it as the fifth rule of its constitution: reads never cross the boundary; writes cross once per transaction; no generated getter calls into the core. The UniFFI and Crux comparison looks at how other tools place themselves among these options. There is a second reason for the rule besides speed. If reads crossed, a core in a web worker or behind a WebSocket during undra dev would need every read to be asynchronous. Because reads are local, the same generated API works in-process, in a worker and over a socket.
