p: Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works
h: Keyed lists: recorded operations, not diffs
x: A list marked #[undra(key = "id")] sends patches made of insert, remove, update, move and clear operations instead of the whole list. The first version of this did not meet its own promise, and the story is in the repository because the benchmark caught it. Originally the core found the patch by comparing the list as it is with a copy of the list as the host last saw it. That comparison hashes every key of both lists and compares surviving rows, so its cost was linear in the list and independent of the change. One insert into an observed 10,000-row list took 536.16 µs, and 85 percent of that was the diff (Finding 1). The store code had known exactly what it did, and that information was thrown away at the Vec and rediscovered at commit. The fix, decided in ADR-027, records the operation instead. Signal<Vec<T>> has push, insert, remove, update_at, move_item and clear. Each mutates the list and appends the wire operation it performed to a log, and a commit sends the log as the patch. The wire did not change. p: Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works
x: An error in a Result<T, E> is a value of a #[undra::error] enum, and it arrives as the platform's natural typed error: Generated by undra bindgen (abbreviated) public enum TodoError: UndraError, Error, Sendable, Hashable { /// The title is empty once spaces are trimmed. case emptyTitle } // store.add(title:) is declared `async throws` and throws a TodoError as itself Generated by undra bindgen (abbreviated) sealed class TodoError(message: String) : UndraException(message) { data object EmptyTitle : TodoError("the title cannot be empty") } TypeScript gets TodoError.EmptyTitle as an Error subclass you can test with instanceof. Replies carry a status byte: ok, typed error, panic, cancelled, stream opened or bad request, and decoders return typed errors for malformed input and never panic. A panic in the core is caught at the dispatch boundary on native targets and answered with a status that carries the panic message and a backtrace. The process is not aborted, the core keeps serving calls, and the log port receives a record at error level or above. Scenario S17 verifies this over JNI and the C ABI. What the host does with that reply is its own policy, and every platform turns it …

p: Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works
x: The core reads no clock and no random source and starts no thread outside the runtime. Time comes from the Clock port, delays from the Timer port, randomness from Rng, the network from Http. That is rule R12. The to-do store shows the discipline: its item identities come from a counter, not from a random source, and after a restore the counter continues above the largest identity in the snapshot. The payoff is testability. In Rust, TestRuntime installs deterministic fakes for every port, including a FakeClock that fires timers when you advance it, and runs the executor on the test thread. On each platform, the contract tests supply a manual clock and an in-memory HTTP server. Scenario S12 advances the clock by 31 seconds to prove that a cached query becomes stale and refetches, without waiting 31 seconds. This is determinism of inputs. It does not make native thread scheduling deterministic, and we do not claim replayability beyond what the tests exercise.

p: Reads never cross the boundary: how Undra's state model works
x: Every design has a price, and the honest version of this post lists it. Memory for copies. An observed keyed list exists in the core, in a baseline copy the core keeps to build patches against, and in the platform mirror. A computed value is sent whole and held in the mirror too. If you observe a large keyed list, you pay for three copies of it. A computed list crosses whole. A keyed Signal<Vec<T>> and a DerivedList<T> get patches. A Computed<Vec<T>> crosses as a full value whenever it changes, so declare a filtered or sorted view of a large list as a DerivedList (ADR-039, added on 2 October 2026), which ships one edited row of a 10,000-row list in 158 bytes where the computed shipped 352.6 KB. A crossing per write. Writes are calls: they encode arguments, cross, and run under the core's single lock. A long synchronous method blocks other callers, so long work belongs in an async method. Every TypeScript method returns a Promise. The O(change) path is opt-in. The recorded list operations are what make patches cheap. A raw update closure is correct and O(list). x: What left loads when it is first needed: stream support, the framed transports' codecs, reconnection, the observe waiters, stats and background runs, the codecs a schema does not name. What stays up front stays for a reason we measured: Keyed-patch merging, because read-your-writes drains are synchronous and could not wait for a chunk. The mirror's compaction, because its backlog bound must hold offline too. Object identity, because every app's first screen waits for it. Connectivity and Lifecycle events, about 530 bytes: a hello core listens to neither, but nothing tells the page so. That needs the core to say when it starts listening, which is an ABI decision with its own record. It is the next lever.

p: Fifteen levers: the JavaScript runtime at 16 KB
x: The adversarial review reproduced the sizes to the byte and found four High defects at the levers' edges: A stripped declaration. reclaim was marked internal, so the published types dropped it, and generated bindings that import it failed tsc against the installed package. Every suite aliased the sources and stayed green. A test now asks the compiler about every name the generator imports. Lost order. snapshot() and restore() ran after an await import(), which yields even when the module is cached, so a call made after restore() reached the core first. They run at the call again. A fetch at the wrong moment. The background drain at pagehide needed a chunk fetched, when a page is being left or is offline and may not be able to fetch one. It calls the core directly now. Codes where data was expected. The production build had turned a WebSocket close reason, which reaches the server, and port errors, which reach the core, into codes. Text that leaves the runtime as data is a sentence in both builds. The fixes cost 131 bytes, to 15,811; smaller fixes and a later merge left the record at 15,774.

p: Undra 1.0: one Rust core under native apps
x: Undra is a Rust framework for the part of an app that is not pixels: its domain logic, reactive state, data layer and persistence. You write that part once, in Rust; Undra generates the Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript that SwiftUI, Compose, React and React Native use, and every screen stays the platform's own. 3 Oct 2026 · 5 min read · Undra team

p: Undra 1.0: one Rust core under native apps
x: An Undra core is a Rust crate. You mark its records, enums, errors and stores with a handful of attributes; the macros describe them as a schema, and undra bindgen turns the schema into the API each platform would write itself: an @Observable class for SwiftUI, StateFlows for Compose, hooks for React and React Native. Each platform keeps a local mirror of the state its screens observe, so a read is a property access and never calls into Rust. A write crosses the boundary once per transaction, and the core answers with one binary change-set that patches every mirror. That is the diagram on the home page, and you can tap it. In a release build on the reference machine, an Apple M5 Pro and not a phone, a synchronous call into the core costs 49.8 ns on the core side, and a change-set of 100 signals 2.3 µs.

p: Undra 1.0: one Rust core under native apps
x: Teams that ship on two or more platforms that must agree on logic, state and data rules: the same validation, the same offline queue, the same cache and when it goes stale, the same answer to "what does this list contain now" on an iPhone, an Android phone and a browser tab. Written three times, those rules drift apart a release at a time. Undra writes them once and leaves each screen as native as it was. It assumes a team that can carry Rust, a real cost that the default-choice post weighs against Kotlin Multiplatform, UniFFI and writing it three times.

x: The core. Records, enums and typed errors; stores of signals and computeds; keyed lists, and derived lists that send only what changed; objects and host callbacks; newtypes, decimals and declared generics. The data layer. Queries and mutations with staleness, retry and optimistic updates that roll back; an offline queue; persistence that migrates stored data across schema changes and refuses what it cannot convert; paged and lazy lists; polling. Ports. Ten platform services with adapters and deterministic fakes; WebSocket, server-sent events and SQLite; the app's own OkHttp, URLSession or fetch underneath. The dev loop. undra dev serves one core to every running app and keeps its state across a rebuild, except in a web page started with npm run dev, which reloads and starts fresh; devtools with a change-set timeline; undra schema diff marks each API change breaking or additive. Platforms. SwiftUI, Compose, React and React Native, built from Xcode, Gradle, Vite or Bazel. iOS 15 and 16 get ObservableObject stores, proven by compilation and a probe on iOS 26.5, not yet on an iOS 15 or 16 runtime, simulator or device. p: Undra vs Kotlin Multiplatform: sharing logic without leaving your platform
x: Undra and Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP) both let you write your domain logic once and keep the screens in SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose and React. They bet on different languages, boundaries and toolchains. We build Undra, so read this with that in mind: every statement about KMP is dated to 30 September 2026 and linked to its source, and one section covers when KMP is the better choice. 30 Sep 2026 · 13 min read · Undra team How to read this page. Statements about KMP describe its state on 30 September 2026 and link to JetBrains' or Google's documentation where one exists. We have not benchmarked KMP and make no numeric claims about it. If something is wrong or has moved, open an issue and we will correct the page with a dated note.

p: Undra vs Kotlin Multiplatform: sharing logic without leaving your platform
x: KMP compiles Kotlin to each target: the JVM and Android, native code for iOS, JavaScript or WebAssembly for the web. Your shared code is Kotlin, it runs in a Kotlin runtime on every platform, and platform code calls into it. Undra compiles Rust to a C ABI library (iOS, and Android through JNI) and to a wasm module (web), and generates Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript from a schema extracted from the Rust. Platform code does not call into your logic to read state; it holds a local mirror. Three differences follow: Language. Kotlin or Rust. For an Android-first team Kotlin is already the daily language. Rust gives you a borrow checker and no garbage collector, and asks more of the people learning it. Boundary. In KMP, platform code reads shared state by calling into the Kotlin runtime. In Undra, reads are local and only writes cross, once per transaction. Scope. KMP is broader: share only logic, or logic and UI with Compose Multiplatform. Undra never shares UI, and ships the state and data layer that KMP leaves to libraries.

p: Undra vs Kotlin Multiplatform: sharing logic without leaving your platform
x: With KMP you write ordinary Kotlin in a common source set and the compiler produces a library per target. Anything Kotlin can express can be shared: models, networking, persistence, view models. Compose Multiplatform extends that to UI; JetBrains lists iOS as Stable and web as Beta (Compose Multiplatform). A shared view model looks like this (illustrative, not from either repository): Illustrative: a KMP shared view model (commonMain) class TodosViewModel(private val repo: TodoRepository) : ViewModel() { private val _state = MutableStateFlow(TodosState()) val state: StateFlow<TodosState> = _state.asStateFlow() fun add(title: String) = viewModelScope.launch { _state.update { it.copy(todos = it.todos + repo.add(title)) } } } With Undra you write a Rust crate and mark what the platforms may see: #[undra::store] for state, #[undra::api] for records, enums and methods, #[undra::query] and #[undra::mutation] for server data, #[undra::port] for things the platform does for you. Undra shares everything under the pixels: stores of signals and computed values, typed errors, a query cache with staleness, deduplication, retry and optimistic updates, an offline queue, persistence, and ports …

p: Undra vs Kotlin Multiplatform: sharing logic without leaving your platform
x: On iOS, Kotlin/Native compiles a shared module into a framework that Swift reaches through an Objective-C header (Kotlin docs). p: Undra vs UniFFI and Crux: three ways to put Rust under a native app
x: UniFFI owns the crossing: it generates the foreign-language side of a Rust library's API. Crux owns the shape of the app: an Elm-style core that never does I/O and a thin shell that does. Undra owns the state that sits between core and screen: signals the UI observes, a data layer, and the loop for developing both. You can stop at any layer. A small Rust library with a handful of functions needs UniFFI and nothing else. An app whose state you want to reason about as a pure function of events may want Crux. Undra is for apps where the hard part is keeping native UI consistent with stateful, server-backed logic on three platforms. Undra does not build on UniFFI or Crux: it has its own wire format and a fixed 19-function C ABI, so nothing below is a statement that one is built on another.

p: Undra vs UniFFI and Crux: three ways to put Rust under a native app
x: UniFFI is Mozilla's toolkit for generating foreign-language bindings for Rust libraries (project). You describe the interface with proc-macros or a UDL file, build a shared library, and run the generator. It has first-party support for Kotlin, Swift and Python (with more limited Ruby support), and third-party bindings exist for others, including JavaScript and WebAssembly, Kotlin Multiplatform, Go and C#. Mozilla uses it extensively in Firefox on mobile and desktop, and describes it as ready for production but a long way from 1.0. Illustrative: UniFFI proc-macro usage uniffi::setup_scaffolding!(); #[derive(uniffi::Record)] pub struct Todo { pub id: u64, pub title: String, pub done: bool } #[uniffi::export] pub fn add_todo(list: Vec<Todo>, title: String) -> Vec<Todo> { /* … */ } The mechanics are the point. UniFFI generates a C-style FFI layer over primitive types. Simple values cross directly; strings, options and records are lowered into a byte buffer the project calls a RustBuffer, and lifted on the other side (how it works). Every call your app makes is an FFI call. The generated Kotlin loads the library through JNA. It supports async functions, callback interfaces and foreign …

p: Undra vs UniFFI and Crux: three ways to put Rust under a native app
x: Crux, maintained by Red Badger, splits an app into a Core in Rust and a Shell in the platform's language (project). The core follows the Elm architecture. You define an Event enum, a Model, a ViewModel and an Effect type, and an update function from event and model to a Command that requests effects. The core never performs I/O. It describes the work as data, the shell performs it and hands the outcome back, and the core continues. A shell is therefore a small loop: send an event, perform each requested effect and resolve it, and read the view model when a render is requested. Its README states that Crux is pre-1.0 and production-ready, with occasional breaking changes, and it links engineering write-ups from Proton and Photoroom. x: This is the deepest architectural difference between Crux and Undra, so it deserves care. In Crux the shell renders a ViewModel. When the core asks for a render, the shell calls view() and receives the whole view model, serialised across the boundary. That is a clean contract: the UI is a function of one value, consistency is trivial, and the view model is easy to assert on in tests. The cost scales with the size of the view model, not the size of the change, and the shell must work out what changed, which SwiftUI and React already do by diffing. For a settings screen this is unremarkable. For a long list that changes one row at a time, the work per update is proportional to the list. Crux is not stuck there. Photoroom's engineering blog describes running into this with a large view model, where the UI could not tell what had changed, and building patches on top: key-path changes generated by diffing view models before and after an update, and sending only those (Photoroom, part 3). In Crux that is something you build; in Undra it is the built-in model. In Undra the state that crosses is per signal, and each platform observes the signals it renders. x: Crux's effects are data: the core requests, the shell performs, the result returns as an event. Its README highlights two consequences. h: When UniFFI is the better choice
x: You want bindings, not a framework. If you have a Rust library and need Swift and Kotlin callers, UniFFI is smaller and simpler to adopt than anything that also brings a runtime. You already have state management on each platform. h: When Crux is the better choice
x: You want Elm's discipline. Every state change is an event, the core is a pure function of events and resolved effects, and tests are plain Rust with no fakes. Some teams find that the most maintainable way to build an app, and Undra does not impose it. Your view models are small and whole-state updates are fine. Then Crux's single-value contract is simpler than signals and patches. You want Rust on the web side too. Crux supports Rust web shells such as Leptos and Yew and lets a Rust shell import the core directly. You need a C# shell. Crux's README says its FFI layer is generated across native, web and C# shells. Undra targets Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript. You want a community with production stories. Crux's README links write-ups from Proton and Photoroom. Undra has a reference app and a test suite, not production mileage. You do not need a built-in data layer. If Http, KeyValue and Time capabilities are enough and you would rather own caching and sync yourself, Crux stays out of the way.

p: Why Undra is the default choice
x: A boundary costs twice: once per crossing, and once for what a crossing carries. Undra's rule is that reads never cross and a write crosses once per transaction, returning one change-set for each store it touched. ADR-031 adds the other half: the platform applies what has arrived once per frame, merged, with a bounded backlog. The number: a burst of 1,667 one-row updates to a 10,000-row list, which is 100,000 a second at 60 Hz, reaches the iOS app as one drain that costs the main thread 787 µs at the median. Applying each update on its own is estimated at 3.4 to 3.94 ms, 20.4 to 23.7 percent of a frame, from the measured cost of one (benchmark results; iPhone 17 Pro simulator on an Apple M5 Pro, so not a device). ADR-044 turned the C ABI into one function table per core, so two cores can share a process without sharing anything. p: Why Undra is the default choice
x: A filtered or sorted view of a big list used to cost the whole list. A Computed<Vec<T>> was recomputed at every commit and sent whole, so one edited row in a 10,000-row list shipped 352.6 KB and took 176.5 µs. A DerivedList (ADR-039) is kept from the source's recorded operations on two order-statistic trees and ships the change: 158 bytes for the same edit, in 333 ns measured on the signals crate directly and 392 ns through the runtime, which is the figure on our landing page; at 100,000 rows, 375 ns and 158 bytes (finding 5; best of three medians). A contract scenario replays 60,000 seeded operations through the Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript runtimes and checks each view's hash after every change-set. What a platform still pays is its own list copy, once per drain: for a one-operation patch to a 100,000-row source, 47 µs in TypeScript and 7 µs in Kotlin. iOS 15 and 16 mode copies the list on every patch, 48 µs at 10,000 rows.

p: Why Undra is the default choice
x: A call that fails does one of three things on every platform: it throws or rejects with the method's own error type, with the platform's cancellation, or with UndraCallError, a closed set of five cases (cancelled by the core, panicked, refused, unavailable, malformed). A command, which has no caller to throw to, reports through onError. No reply status, cancellation or lost connection reaches fatalError, an uncaught exception or an unhandled rejection (docs/ERRORS.md, ADR-032). A native panic is caught at the boundary and arrives as panicked, and the app's onPanic receives a structured report with frames its crash reporter can symbolicate (ADR-046); a computed that panics poisons only itself (ADR-019); a stream's failure is a typed item on the wire (ADR-036); a write from a thread the runtime does not own is refused in every build (ADR-035). A wasm core cannot unwind, so it traps; with crashRecovery() the runtime restarts the same module and restores the last snapshot (ADR-049, docs). The number: 3.12 to 3.22 ms at the median from the trap to a running core, with a 100 KB state, over five runs in headless Chromium (benchmark results). Recovery is opt-in, and a call in flight at …

p: Why Undra is the default choice
x: Edit Rust, save, and the app on a simulator, an emulator or a page reconnects by itself, with exponential backoff from 250 ms to 5 s, and observes its stores again (ADR-051). The core's state is snapshotted in memory before the rebuild and restored into the new core before it listens, so the app returns to the screen it was on, and the dev bar says "Reloaded, state kept" or why not (ADR-053). A screen that shows a query is carried too: its query handle comes back on the same handle and fetches with the code that was just rebuilt, with no code in the app for the handle (a value the app set by a call outside its stores, such as a server’s address, is told to the new core again; ADR-059). The number: the playground's 204 KiB snapshot restores in 1.6 ms inside undra dev, which runs a debug build of the core (189 µs in a release build), and 74 ms pass from suspending the old core to the new one listening (the piece's record). A page served by undra dev shows every store's live value and a timeline of every change-set, and a scrubber restores the core to an earlier step while the app follows (ADR-054, docs/DEV_LOOP.md). It sits behind a per-run token.

p: Why Undra is the default choice
h: Shipping an update, and shipping the app
x: Persisted data records the structure it was written with, so a build that changed a type still reads what the last one stored: by name for free, through a #[undra::migrate] hook when a name changed, and never by discarding it silently (ADR-037, Shipping an update). A queued write the new build cannot carry over becomes a dead letter the app can show. Storage ports fail with typed errors (full, locked, corrupt, unavailable, io) on every platform instead of raw throws (ADR-049). The number: the hello-world web core is 113.1 KB gzipped against a 120 KB budget, and the JavaScript a hello-world page loads up front is 15.8 KB gzipped against a 16 KB budget, for the production build of the runtime as an app installs it, with Vite's own preload helper reported beside it and gated on its own. CI fails a change that exceeds either (ADR-052, size record). Opt-in pieces stay out of the hello world: the remote transport and the default ports load on first use, and the browser database adds about 299 KB gzipped, only to an app that imports it.

L2, one feature: one screen's state and requests become a store, a query and a mutation. p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: Cross-platform tools fall into two camps. One shares the pixels: you write the UI once and a toolkit puts it on every platform. The other shares what is under the pixels and lets each platform draw its own screens. Undra is in the second camp, and this post explains why without pretending the first camp is wrong. Shared UI is the right answer for many products, and we say which. 30 Sep 2026 · 9 min read · Undra team How to read this page. We build Undra, a framework that shares logic and never UI, so we have a stake in this argument. Statements about Flutter, React Native and Compose Multiplatform describe them on 30 September 2026 and link to their own documentation. If you think we have misrepresented one, open an issue.

p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: The first bet is that the UI is the expensive part, so share it. Three mature tools make this bet in different ways. Flutter has its own rendering engine, Impeller, and its own implementations of each UI control rather than deferring to the system's (architecture overview). You write Dart, and Flutter paints its own widgets with its own engine. React Native turns a tree of React components into the platform's own views: a UIView on iOS, an android.view.ViewGroup or android.widget.TextView on Android (render pipeline). You write JavaScript or TypeScript and the screen is made of host views. Its New Architecture has been the default since React Native 0.76 (docs). Compose Multiplatform takes Jetpack Compose to other platforms. JetBrains lists iOS as Stable and web as Beta and describes interop that lets you keep existing SwiftUI or Android View code (product page). Its FAQ says the components are drawn on a canvas rather than being platform widgets (FAQ). The second bet is that the logic is the expensive part, so share that and keep the UI native. p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: The benefits are large and we do not want to undersell them. One UI codebase. One set of screens, one set of UI tests, one design system implementation. A small team ships to several platforms with the headcount of one. Consistency by construction. The same screen behaves the same way everywhere, which matters when the product's identity is its own look and not the platform's. Iteration speed. These toolkits put a lot of effort into fast feedback loops for UI work, and a single codebase means a fix lands everywhere at once. Fit with your existing skills. A team that already writes React can reach mobile through React Native. A Kotlin team can reach iOS through Compose Multiplatform. Shared UI is usually the right choice when any of these describes the product: A small team or a startup that needs to reach several platforms quickly. A brand-led or highly custom interface, where a bespoke look matters more than platform convention. An internal tool or a content app where the screens are simple and the platform's idioms are not a selling point. p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: The trade is not the same for each toolkit, and none of it is fatal. It is a set of costs that show up at the edges, and the costs are different if you start from a native app than if you start from nothing. Platform idioms. Native controls bring platform behaviour with them: text selection, scroll physics, navigation transitions, keyboard handling, system sheets and menus. React Native inherits much of this because its screens are host views. Flutter and Compose Multiplatform draw their own controls, so matching a platform convention is the toolkit's work, or yours. Brand-led apps often do not want a match, which is the point of the first bet. Day-one OS features. When a platform ships a new UI API, native code can adopt it with the new SDK. A shared toolkit adopts it on its own schedule, or you embed a native view. Flutter documents platform views for exactly this, and notes that synchronising them with Flutter's rendering carries overhead, so it recommends them for complex controls where reimplementing is impractical. p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: Undra draws the line exactly at the UI. Everything under it is shared: domain logic, reactive state, the data layer, persistence and the dev loop. Everything above it stays a hand-written SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose or React screen. Our reasoning starts from where the work repeats. In our experience the code beneath the UI is where the three platforms disagree and where the subtle bugs live: the cache, the retry policy, the offline queue, pagination, the session refresh. Teams write these three times and get three slightly different answers. The screens, by contrast, are where platform expertise pays off. So Undra shares the part that must be identical and leaves the part that should feel native. The bar is that a SwiftUI view bound to Undra state is indistinguishable from one bound to Swift state. That is achievable because the generated store is an ordinary @Observable class, a Kotlin StateFlow or a TypeScript Signal. p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
h: Why not share the UI too?
x: We considered it and rejected it, for a reason that is about focus more than principle. Flutter, React Native and Compose Multiplatform are whole-UI products, each maintained by a large team that chases every platform's new UI features, keeps accessibility in step and polishes rendering. An Undra UI toolkit would be a smaller and later version of one of them, and it would be the part of Undra most likely to age badly. The moment a framework paints pixels on three platforms it takes on that ongoing work, and it inherits the trade-offs listed above. There is also a practical reason. If the UI stays native, Undra's generated code has a clear bar to meet: a Swift, Kotlin or TypeScript engineer who has never seen Rust must be able to review it and find it idiomatic. The golden files that lock the generated output are how the project holds itself to that bar.

p: Why Undra keeps your UI native
x: Drawing the line here has costs, and they are the mirror image of what shared UI buys. You build three UIs. That means three implementations of the design, three UI test suites, and keeping the screens from drifting apart. If your product needs pixel-identical screens, this is the wrong tool. You need Rust. The core is Rust. Undra's macros emit errors that say what, why, how to fix it and where to read more, and they keep lifetimes and threads off the common path, but the borrow checker remains, and in our experience most mobile teams have few Rust engineers. Only the people writing the core need it; the platform teams consume generated Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript. Logic must be worth sharing. If your app is mostly UI with little logic beneath it, sharing the logic buys little. The worst case for Undra is an app that is 90 percent UI and 10 percent logic. It is a new framework.
